questions.question_text:
The table shows the number of batches of cookies made, $b$, and the flour used, $F$ (in kg).
Does this table show direct variation, inverse variation, or neither?
If it shows variation, write the equation.
$\begin{array}{c|cccc} b & 2 & 3 & 5 & 8 \\ \hline F & 5 & 7.5 & 12.5 & 20 \end{array}$

options.why: Tested the product $bF$ instead of the ratio $F/b$, and misclassified a constant ratio as inverse variation.

options.text: Neither — the values don't form a clear pattern
options.why: Failed to compute the ratio $F/b$ for each pair, which is in fact constant at $2.5$.
Used the first row's $F$-value as the constant instead of dividing $F$ by $b$.

questions.solution_text:
$\dfrac{F}{b}: 5\div2=2.5,\ 7.5\div3=2.5,\ 12.5\div5=2.5,\ 20\div8=2.5$
The ratio is constant for every pair, so this is direct variation.
$k=2.5$, so $F=2.5b$.

questions.question_text:
The table shows the number of winners, $n$, sharing a fixed prize pool and the amount each winner receives, $s$ (in dollars).
Does this table show direct variation, inverse variation, or neither?
If it shows variation, write the equation.
$\begin{array}{c|cccc} n & 4 & 5 & 8 & 10 \\ \hline s & 300 & 240 & 150 & 120 \end{array}$

options.why: Tested the ratio $s/n$ instead of the product $ns$, then misread the actual constant product as a ratio.

options.text: Neither — $s$ decreases but not by a fixed rule
options.why: Did not test the product $ns$ for each pair, which is in fact constant at $1200$.
Inverted the equation, placing $n$ in the numerator instead of the constant of variation.

questions.solution_text:
$ns: 4\times300=1200,\ 5\times240=1200,\ 8\times150=1200,\ 10\times120=1200$
The product is constant for every pair, so this is inverse variation.
$k=1200$, so $s=\dfrac{1200}{n}$.

questions.question_text:
Does this table show direct variation, inverse variation, or neither?
$\begin{array}{c|cccc} x & 2 & 3 & 5 & 6 \\ \hline y & 7 & 10 & 16 & 19 \end{array}$

options.why: Used only the first pair's ratio, $7\div2$ rounded to $3$, without checking it stays constant across the rest of the table.
Used only the first pair's product, $2\times7=14$, without checking it stays constant across the rest of the table.
Used only the first pair's exact ratio ($7\div2=3.5$) without checking whether it holds for every other pair.

questions.solution_text:
$\dfrac{y}{x}: 7\div2=3.5,\ 10\div3\neq3.5$
The ratio is not constant, so this is not direct variation.
$xy: 2\times7=14,\ 3\times10=30$
The product is not constant either, so this is not inverse variation.
This table shows neither direct nor inverse variation.

questions.question_text:
Does this table show direct variation, inverse variation, or neither?
$\begin{array}{c|cccc} x & 3 & 6 & 9 & 12 \\ \hline y & 12 & 24 & 36 & 50 \end{array}$

options.text: Neither — the ratio $y/x$ is constant for the first three pairs but not the last

options.why: Checked only the first three pairs and stopped, missing that the last pair breaks the constant ratio.

options.text: Inverse variation; the values must fit since three pairs agree
options.why: Did not test the product $xy$ at all, and assumed matching behaviour on most pairs is enough to confirm variation.
Averaged the ratios across all four pairs instead of checking whether the ratio is exactly constant.

questions.solution_text:
$\dfrac{y}{x}: 12\div3=4,\ 24\div6=4,\ 36\div9=4,\ 50\div12=4.1\overline{6}$
The first three pairs give a ratio of $4$, but the last pair does not, so the ratio is not constant across every pair.
$xy: 3\times12=36,\ 6\times24=144$
The product is not constant either, so this is not inverse variation.
This table shows neither direct nor inverse variation — every pair must be checked, not just the first few.

questions.question_text:
The table below lists $(x,y)$ pairs, not in order of increasing $x$.
Does this table show direct variation, inverse variation, or neither?
If it shows variation, write the equation.
$\begin{array}{c|cccc} x & 4 & 10 & 2 & 6 \\ \hline y & 6 & 15 & 3 & 9 \end{array}$

options.text: Neither — the $x$-values aren't in order, so no pattern can be tested
options.why: Assumed a table must be sorted by $x$ before the ratio or product tests can be applied, which isn't required.
Correctly found a constant value from the ratio test but misclassified it as belonging to the inverse-variation product test.
Used the first row's $y$-value directly as the constant of variation instead of dividing by the matching $x$-value.

questions.solution_text:
$\dfrac{y}{x}: 6\div4=1.5,\ 15\div10=1.5,\ 3\div2=1.5,\ 9\div6=1.5$
Even though the $x$-values are not listed in order, the ratio is still checked for every pair and is constant, so this is direct variation.
$k=1.5$, so $y=1.5x$.

questions.question_text:
Does this table show direct variation, inverse variation, or neither?
$\begin{array}{c|cccc} x & 3 & 3 & 5 & 7 \\ \hline y & 9 & 12 & 15 & 21 \end{array}$

options.text: Neither — $x=3$ is paired with two different $y$-values

options.why: Used only the pair $x=3,y=9$ to find the ratio and ignored that $x=3$ is also paired with $y=12$.
Used only the pair $x=3,y=9$ to find the product and ignored that $x=3$ is also paired with a different $y$-value.

options.text: Neither — the ratio $y/x$ is not constant, since $(5,15)$ and $(7,21)$ give different ratios
options.why: Compared the wrong pairs — $(5,15)$ and $(7,21)$ both give a ratio of $3$; the real inconsistency is that $x=3$ has two different $y$-values, not a ratio mismatch between those two pairs.

questions.solution_text:
The value $x=3$ is paired with two different $y$-values, $y=9$ and $y=12$.
A table of direct or inverse variation must give exactly one $y$-value for each $x$-value, so this table cannot show any variation.
This table shows neither direct nor inverse variation.

questions.question_text:
A table gives $x=3,5,6$ paired with $y=20,12,10$.
A fourth measurement then records $x=15$, $y=5$.
Is this fourth measurement consistent with the same variation relationship shown by the rest of the table?
$\begin{array}{c|ccc} x & 3 & 5 & 6 \\ \hline y & 20 & 12 & 10 \end{array}$

options.text: No — the relationship is inverse variation with $k=60$, but $15\times5=75\neq60$
Yes — the relationship is inverse variation with $k=60$, and $15\times5=60$
options.why: Made an arithmetic slip multiplying $15\times5$, computing $60$ instead of the correct $75$.

options.text: No — the relationship is direct variation, and the fourth pair doesn't fit
options.why: Misclassified the original table as direct variation by testing only the ratio $y/x$, which is not constant, instead of the product.

options.text: Yes — any new pair is automatically consistent once three pairs agree
options.why: Assumed agreement among the first three pairs guarantees any further pair fits, without actually checking the new pair against $k$.

questions.solution_text:
$\dfrac{y}{x}: 20\div3\neq12\div5$
The ratio is not constant, so this is not direct variation.
$xy: 3\times20=60,\ 5\times12=60,\ 6\times10=60$
The product is constant for the first three pairs, so this is inverse variation with $k=60$.
Checking the fourth pair: $15\times5=75$, which does not match $k=60$.
The fourth pair is not consistent with the same inverse variation relationship.

questions.question_text: Which one of the relationships shown below is NOT directly proportional?

options.why: Each ratio $y/x$ equals 4, so this relationship is directly proportional.
Each ratio $y/x$ equals 2.5, so this relationship is directly proportional.
Each ratio $y/x$ equals 1.5, so this relationship is directly proportional.

questions.solution_text: For option C, the ratios are $9/2=4.5$, $36/8=4.5$, and $70/14=5$. Since the ratio is not constant, it is not directly proportional.
